summary: Specifies an RTP payload format for the Variable-Rate Multimode Wideband (VMR-WB) speech codec and registers a media type for it. The format is designed to interoperate with existing VMR-WB transport formats on non-IP networks. It is standards-track and was updated by RFC 4424.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4348 says how to put VMR-WB speech into RTP packets. VMR-WB is a wideband speech codec used in CDMA mobile networks, and its third mode produces exactly the same bytes as the AMR-WB codec used in other mobile networks. This document defines two ways to carry those bytes over IP: a minimal one that sends a single frame per packet, and a richer one with a table of contents that can bundle several frames and interleave them so that a lost packet hurts less.

questions: how is vmr-wb carried over rtp
what is the vmr-wb header-free payload format
what is the cmr field in rtp audio
subtitle: How to pack VMR-WB wideband speech frames into RTP packets, including a header-free mode and a gateway-friendly octet-aligned mode.

tldr.problem: There was no agreed way to carry the VMR-WB wideband speech codec over RTP, so a gateway could not pass speech between a CDMA network and an IP network without transcoding it.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines two payload formats. The header-free format puts one speech frame straight into each packet. The octet-aligned format adds a small header, a table of contents and optional frame interleaving, and its interoperable mode is byte for byte the AMR-WB format.
tldr.outcome: Speech can cross between VMR-WB and AMR-WB systems without being decoded and re-encoded. RFC 4348 was later updated by RFC 4424.

today: RFC 4348 was published in January 2006 as a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 4424. It remains the registered way to carry VMR-WB speech over RTP.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The document specifies the payload format for packetization of VMR-WB-encoded speech signals into the Real-time Transport Protocol. The VMR-WB payload formats support transmission of single and multiple channels, frame interleaving, multiple frames per payload, header-free payload, the use of mode switching, and interoperation with existing VMR-WB transport formats on non-IP networks.

The VMR-WB file format, that is for transport of VMR-WB speech data in storage mode applications such as email, is specified separately. A media type registration for the VMR-WB RTP payload format is provided in section 9.

VMR-WB is a variable-rate multimode wideband speech codec that has a number of operating modes, one of which is interoperable with the AMR-WB audio codec at certain rates. Provisions have therefore been made in this document to facilitate and simplify data packet exchange between VMR-WB and AMR-WB in the interoperable mode with no transcoding function involved.

Since VMR-WB is interoperable with AMR-WB at certain rates, an attempt has been made throughout the document to maximize the similarities with RFC 3267 while optimizing the payload format for the non-interoperable modes of the VMR-WB codec.

The document uses the term interoperable mode for VMR-WB mode 3, which is interoperable with AMR-WB codec modes 0, 1 and 2, and the term non-interoperable modes for VMR-WB modes 0, 1 and 2. The term frame-block describes the time-synchronized set of speech frames in a multi-channel VMR-WB session. In an N-channel session, a frame-block contains N speech frames, one from each of the channels, and all N speech frames represent exactly the same time period.
sections.plainLanguage: The point of the exercise is that the same speech bytes can be understood by both codecs. If the two ends can agree on the mode, no transcoding is needed anywhere along the path.

sections.title: The VMR-WB Speech Codec
sections.content:
VMR-WB is the wideband speech-coding standard developed by the Third Generation Partnership Project 2 for encoding and decoding wideband and narrowband speech content in multimedia services in 3G CDMA cellular systems. It is a source-controlled variable-rate multimode wideband speech codec. It has a number of operating modes, where each mode is a tradeoff between voice quality and average data rate. The operating mode is chosen based on the traffic condition of the network and the desired quality of service. The desired average data rate in each mode is obtained by encoding speech frames at permissible rates compliant with the CDMA2000 system, depending on the instantaneous characteristics of the input speech and the maximum and minimum rate constraints imposed by the network operator.

While VMR-WB is a native CDMA codec complying with all CDMA system requirements, it is further interoperable with AMR-WB at 12.65, 8.85 and 6.60 kbps, because the two share the same core technology. This feature enables Transcoder-Free interconnections between VMR-WB and AMR-WB across different wireless and wireline systems, without unnecessary media format conversion.

The permissible encoding rates are full-rate at 13.3 kbps with a frame size of 266 bits, half-rate at 6.2 kbps with 124 bits, quarter-rate at 2.7 kbps with 54 bits, eighth-rate at 1.0 kbps with 20 bits, and blank and erasure frame types with no bits.

VMR-WB is able to transition between various modes with no degradation in voice quality attributable to the switching itself. The operating mode of the encoder may be switched seamlessly without prior knowledge of the decoder. In the interoperable mode, mode switching between VMR-WB modes is not allowed, because there is only one AMR-WB interoperable mode in VMR-WB. In-band data included in the VMR-WB frame structure is used during an interoperable interconnection to switch between VMR-WB frame types 0, 1 and 2 in mode 3.

VMR-WB can operate with either 16000-Hz or 8000-Hz sampled input and output speech signals in all modes of operation. The decoder does not require prior knowledge about the sampling rate of the original media, and by default generates 16000-Hz wideband output regardless of the encoder input sampling frequency. While the specification defines a 16000-Hz RTP clock rate for the codec, the injection and processing of 8000-Hz narrowband media during a session is allowed; a 16000-Hz RTP clock rate MUST always be used.

The circuit-switched operation of VMR-WB within a CDMA network requires continuous transmission of speech data during a conversation. VMR-WB does, however, have the capability to operate in a discontinuous transmission mode for some packet-switched applications over IP networks, where the number of transmitted bits and packets during a silence period is reduced to a minimum. The VMR-WB DTX operation is similar to that of AMR-WB.
sections.plainLanguage: The codec has several modes, each a different quality and a different average bit rate. The sender picks the mode to suit the network at that moment, and it can change mode mid-call without telling the receiver first.

sections.title: Robustness against Packet Loss
sections.content:
The octet-aligned payload format supports forward error correction and frame interleaving, in order to increase robustness against lost packets.

The simple scheme of repetition of previously sent data is one way of achieving FEC. In this repetition method, previously transmitted frame-blocks are retransmitted together with the current frame-block or blocks, using a sliding window to group the speech frame-blocks to send in each payload. In the example given, each frame-block is retransmitted one time in the following RTP payload packet. The use of this approach does not require signaling at the session setup, because a packet containing redundant frames does not look different from a packet with only new frames. The receiver may receive multiple copies or versions of a frame for a certain timestamp if no packet is lost, and if multiple versions of the same speech frame are received it is RECOMMENDED that the highest rate be used by the speech decoder. This redundancy scheme provides the same functionality as RFC 2198, and in most cases the mechanism in this payload format is more efficient and simpler than requiring both endpoints to support RFC 2198. If the spread in time required between the primary and redundant encodings is larger than 5 frame times, the bandwidth overhead of RFC 2198 will be lower.

The sender is responsible for selecting an appropriate amount of redundancy based on feedback about the channel, for example in RTCP receiver reports, or on network traffic. A sender SHOULD NOT base the selection of FEC on the CMR, as this parameter most probably was set based on non-IP information. The sender is also responsible for avoiding congestion, which may be aggravated by redundant transmission.

To decrease protocol overhead, the octet-aligned payload format allows several speech frame-blocks to be encapsulated into a single RTP packet. One of the drawbacks is that in case of packet loss several consecutive speech frame-blocks are lost, which usually causes clearly audible distortion. Interleaving improves speech quality in such cases by distributing the consecutive losses into a series of single frame-block losses. Interleaving and bundling several frame-blocks per payload increase end-to-end delay and are therefore not appropriate for all types of applications. Streaming applications will most likely be able to exploit interleaving to improve speech quality in lossy transmission conditions. For the encoder to use frame interleaving in its outbound RTP packets for a given session, the decoder needs to indicate its support by out-of-band means.
sections.plainLanguage: Two tricks make a lost packet less damaging. One is to send an older copy of the speech along with the new one, so the receiver has a spare. The other is to spread the frames out so that one lost packet takes out scattered frames instead of a run of them.

sections.title: RTP Header Usage
sections.content:
The format of the RTP header is specified in RFC 3550, and this payload format uses the fields of the header in a manner consistent with that specification.

The RTP timestamp corresponds to the sampling instant of the first sample encoded for the first frame-block in the packet. The timestamp clock frequency is the same as the default sampling frequency, 16 kHz, so the timestamp unit is in samples. The duration of one speech frame-block is 20 ms for VMR-WB. For normal wideband operation the input and output media sampling frequency is 16 kHz, corresponding to 320 samples per frame from each channel, so the timestamp is increased by 320 for each consecutive frame-block. Because the payload formats for 8 and 16 kHz sampled media are identical and the decoder does not need prior knowledge of the encoder input sampling frequency, a fixed RTP clock rate of 16000 Hz is defined for the VMR-WB codec. The timestamp is incremented by 320 per frame-block for 8 kHz sampled media as well.

A packet may contain multiple frame-blocks of encoded speech or comfort noise parameters. If interleaving is employed, the frame-blocks encapsulated into a payload are picked according to the interleaving rules. Otherwise, each packet covers a period of one or more contiguous 20 ms frame-block intervals.

No matter which payload format is used, the RTP payload is always made an integral number of octets long by padding with zero bits if necessary. If additional padding is required, then the P bit in the RTP header MAY be set and padding appended, as specified in RFC 3550.

The RTP header marker bit SHALL be always set to 0 if the VMR-WB codec operates in continuous transmission. When operating in discontinuous transmission, the marker bit SHALL be set to 1 if the first frame-block carried in the packet contains a speech frame, which is the first in a talkspurt. For all other packets, the marker bit SHALL be set to zero.
sections.plainLanguage: The timestamp counts samples at 16 kHz, and each 20 ms frame-block advances it by 320. The marker bit marks the first packet of a burst of speech when the codec is not sending anything during silence.

sections.title: The Header-Free Payload Format
sections.content:
For a given session, the payload format can be either header-free or octet aligned, depending on the mode of operation established for the session by out-of-band means and the application.

The header-free payload format is designed for maximum bandwidth efficiency, simplicity and minimum delay. Only one speech data frame is present in each header-free payload format packet. None of the payload header fields or table of contents entries is present. The encoding rate for the speech frame can be determined from the length of the speech data frame, since there is only one speech data frame in each header-free payload format.

The use of the RTP header fields for the header-free payload format is the same as for the octet-aligned payload format. The detailed bit mapping of speech data packets permissible for this payload format is described in section 8 of the VMR-WB standard specification. Since the header-free payload format is not compatible with the AMR-WB RTP payload, only non-interoperable modes of VMR-WB SHALL be used with it. That is, frame types 0, 1, 2 and 9 SHALL NOT be used with the header-free payload format.

The mode of operation is decided by the transmitting, or encoder, site. The default mode of operation for a VMR-WB encoder is mode 0. The mode change request may also be sent through non-RTP means, which is out of the scope of this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The simplest form puts the encoded speech straight into the packet with nothing in front of it. The receiver works out the bit rate from the length of the data. It cannot be used with the interoperable mode.

sections.title: The Octet-Aligned Payload Format
sections.content:
In the octet-aligned payload format, all the fields in a payload, including the payload header, table of contents entries and the speech frames themselves, are individually aligned to octet boundaries to make implementations efficient. Octet alignment of a field means that the last octet is padded with zeroes in the least significant bits to fill the octet, and this padding is separate from the padding indicated by the P bit in the RTP header. Between the two payload formats, only the octet-aligned format has the capability to use interleaving. The VMR-WB octet-aligned payload format in the interoperable mode is identical to that of AMR-WB.

The complete payload consists of a payload header, a payload table of contents, and speech data representing one or more speech frame-blocks.

The payload header consists of a 4-bit CMR, 4 reserved bits, and, optionally, an 8-bit interleaving header. The CMR indicates a codec mode request sent to the speech encoder at the site of the receiver of the payload. CMR value 15 indicates that no mode request is present, and other unused values are reserved. CMR values 0, 1 and 2 request VMR-WB mode 3 at 6.60, 8.85 and 12.65 kbps, CMR 3 requests mode 2, CMR 4 requests mode 1, CMR 5 requests mode 0, and CMR 6 requests mode 2 with maximum half-rate encoding. The R bits are reserved, MUST be set to zero and MUST be ignored by the receiver.

The ILL field is an optional 4-bit unsigned integer present only if interleaving is signaled out-of-band for the session. ILL equals L indicates to the receiver that the interleaving length is L+1 frame-blocks. The ILP field is an optional 4-bit unsigned integer present only if interleaving is signaled. ILP MUST take a value between 0 and ILL inclusive, indicating the interleaving index for frame-blocks in this payload in the interleave group. If ILP is found greater than ILL, the payload SHOULD be discarded. ILL and ILP fields MUST be present in each packet in a session if interleaving is signaled for the session. The mode request received in the CMR field is valid until the next CMR is received. If a payload is received with a CMR value that is not valid, the CMR MUST be ignored by the receiver. The CMR field MUST be set to 15 for packets sent to a multicast group.

The table of contents consists of a list of ToC entries, each representing a speech frame. Each entry is one octet: a 1-bit F flag that says whether another frame follows, a 4-bit FT frame type index, a 1-bit Q frame quality indicator, and 3 padding bits that MUST be set to zero and ignored by a receiver. Frame types 14 and 15 mean a lost frame and a blank frame, and no data octets are present for them in the payload. If a payload with an invalid FT value is received, the payload MUST be discarded. For multi-channel sessions, with N channels and K speech frame-blocks in a packet, there MUST be N*K entries in the ToC, with the first N entries from the first frame-block and so on.

Speech data of a payload contains one or more speech frames as described in the ToC. Each speech frame represents 20 ms of speech encoded in one of the available encoding rates. The last octet of each speech frame MUST be padded with zeroes so that each speech frame is octet-aligned, and when multiple speech frames are present they MUST be arranged one whole frame after another. The speech frames are packed in the same order as their corresponding ToC entries are arranged in the ToC list.

The frame types are listed in table 3 of the document. Frame type 0 is the interoperable full rate at 6.60 kbps with a frame size of 132 bits, 1 is 8.85 kbps with 177 bits, 2 is 12.65 kbps with 253 bits, 3 is full rate at 13.3 kbps with 266 bits, 4 is half rate at 6.2 kbps with 124 bits, 5 is quarter rate at 2.7 kbps with 54 bits, 6 is eighth rate at 1.0 kbps with 20 bits, 9 is comfort noise with 40 bits, 14 is erasure with no bits and 15 is blank with no bits. The remaining values are reserved.
sections.plainLanguage: The richer format starts with one or two octets of header, then a list of one-octet entries saying what each frame is and how long it is, then the frames themselves. Because everything is on octet boundaries, an implementation can walk the packet without doing bit arithmetic.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RTP packets using this payload format are subject to the general security considerations discussed in RTP and any applicable profile such as AVP or SAVP. As this format transports encoded audio, the main security issues include confidentiality, integrity protection and data origin authentication of the audio itself. The payload format itself does not have any built-in security mechanisms, and any suitable external mechanism, such as SRTP, MAY be used.

This payload format and the VMR-WB decoder do not exhibit any significant non-uniformity in the receiver-side computational complexity for packet processing, so they are unlikely to pose a denial-of-service threat due to the receipt of pathological data.

To ensure confidentiality of the encoded audio, all audio data bits MUST be encrypted. There is less need to encrypt the payload header or the table of contents, since they only carry information about the frame type, which could also be useful to a third party for quality monitoring. The use of interleaving in conjunction with encryption can have a negative impact on confidentiality for a short period of time, because frames 17, 18 and 21 have been supplied in prior packets under the prior key, and error concealment may make the audio intelligible at least as far as frame 18 or 19.

To authenticate the sender of the speech, an external mechanism MUST be used, and it is RECOMMENDED that such a mechanism protects both the complete RTP header and the payload. Data tampering by a man-in-the-middle attacker could replace audio content and also result in erroneous depacketization and decoding that could lower the audio quality. Tampering with the CMR field, for example, may result in speech of a different quality than desired.
sections.plainLanguage: The format carries no protection of its own. Encrypt the speech bits and authenticate the packets with something outside it, such as SRTP. One catch: interleaving spreads frames across packets, so changing the key does not immediately hide the speech that has already been sent.

sections.title: Payload Format Parameters
sections.content:
The parameters are defined as part of the MIME subtype registration for the VMR-WB speech codec. The MIME subtype is allocated from the IETF tree, with media type name audio and media subtype name VMR-WB. There are no required parameters. The receiver MUST ignore any unspecified parameter and use the default values instead.

The optional parameters are mode-set, a comma-separated list of integers restricting the active operating modes to a subset of modes 0, 1, 2 and 3; channels, the number of audio channels, defaulting to 1 if omitted; octet-align, which is 1 when the octet-aligned payload format SHALL be used and 0 or absent for the header-free format; maxptime; interleaving, whose value defines the maximum number of frame-blocks allowed in an interleaving group and whose presence implies octet-aligned operation; ptime, which SHALL be at least one frame size for VMR-WB; and dtx, which is 0 by default and 1 when the codec operates in discontinuous transmission mode with silence descriptor frames sent during silence intervals. If the interleaving parameter is present, the parameter octet-align=1 MUST also be present. The intended usage is Common.

The mapping into SDP is as follows. The media type audio goes in the SDP m= line as the media name. The media subtype goes in a=rtpmap as the encoding name, and the RTP clock rate in a=rtpmap MUST be 16000 for VMR-WB. The channels parameter MUST be either explicitly set to N or omitted, implying a default value of 1, and if present is specified after the MIME subtype and RTP clock rate in the a=rtpmap attribute. The ptime and maxptime parameters go in the a=ptime and a=maxptime attributes. Any remaining parameters go in the a=fmtp attribute, copied directly from the MIME media type string as a semicolon-separated list of parameter and value pairs.

In an offer-answer negotiation, the rate, channel and payload configuration parameters octet-align and interleaving SHALL be used symmetrically, so the offer and the answer must use the same values. The maximum size of the interleaving buffer is declarative, and each agent specifies the value it supports to receive. The mode-set parameter is declarative too, and only operating modes indicated as supported by both ends SHALL be used. If the answerer supports none of the operating modes in the offer, the complete payload type declaration SHOULD be rejected by removing it from the answer.
sections.plainLanguage: The session description carries the same information as the media type does. The two ends must agree on the format and the channel count, and each says which codec modes it can handle, so that only modes both support are used.

fields.name: CMR
fields.desc: Codec mode request sent to the encoder at the receiver.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Reserved bits. They must be set to zero and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: CMR
fields.desc: Codec mode request. Value 15 means no request is present.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Reserved bits, set to zero and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: ILL
fields.desc: Interleaving length, present only when interleaving is signalled.

fields.name: ILP
fields.desc: Interleaving index, present only when interleaving is signalled.

items.label: Interoperable full rate
items.desc: AMR-WB at 6.60 kbps, frame size 132 bits.

items.label: Interoperable full rate
items.desc: AMR-WB at 8.85 kbps, frame size 177 bits.

items.label: Interoperable full rate
items.desc: AMR-WB at 12.65 kbps, frame size 253 bits.

items.label: CNG
items.desc: Comfort noise, the AMR-WB silence descriptor, frame size 40 bits.

items.label: Erasure
items.desc: AMR-WB SPEECH_LOST. No data octets are present.

items.label: Blank
items.desc: AMR-WB NO_DATA. No data octets are present.
